title: Stop Doing the 90-day recomp Wrong: Train Your total body recomposition Instead
description: Bulking will fatten you and cutting will shrink you. There is a third road built exactly for the skinny fat body: recomposition. Take your day-zero baseline, learn how energy partitioning works, and get the ninety-day method that trains it.

scenes.narration: Before any method, a baseline. Take your front and side photos in the same light you will use on day ninety. Measure your waist at the navel. Then do one max set of push-ups, clean reps only, and write down all three numbers: waist, weight, push-ups. These are not there to judge you. They are the instruments that will judge the method. A recomp is quiet work; the scale barely moves and the mirror lies on a daily basis, so the numbers are how you will know the truth. The push-up max matters more than people think: it is your strength witness. If it climbs month after month while your waist shrinks, the recomp is working, whatever the scale says. Keep your three numbers somewhere safe. At the end I will show you how to read them like a coach.

scenes.label: PHOTOS, WAIST, ONE MAX SET
scenes.sub: no baseline, no proof - measure before you start
scenes.narration: Here is why day zero matters so much for this method. Recomposition is the slowest-looking transformation there is in its first month, and the most dramatic by its third. Without a baseline, month one feels like nothing is happening, and most guys quit a working plan. With photos and a waist number from day zero, the same month shows a centimetre gone and five push-ups gained, and the plan survives. The baseline is not paperwork. It is the thing that keeps you in the game long enough for the method to pay you.

The engine of recomposition has a name: energy partitioning. It answers one question: when energy and protein arrive in your body, where do they go? To fat storage, or to muscle building? Three things steer the answer. First, the training signal: a muscle that was trained hard recently becomes greedy, pulling in glucose and amino acids for days. Second, protein supply: building material has to be present when the order arrives. Third, your starting point: an untrained body with some fat stored is unusually willing to fund muscle growth partly from its own stores. Eat around maintenance, maybe a touch under, train hard three or four days a week, hit your protein, and the partitioning tilts your way. You are not eating for two goals. You are steering one flow of energy toward the address that builds you. That steering, repeated for ninety days, is the entire method.

Two levers do almost all the steering, so let us put numbers on them. Lever one is protein: around 1.6 grams per kilogram of your bodyweight per day is the range where research keeps landing for building muscle. For a seventy-kilo guy that is roughly one hundred and ten grams, spread across the day, every day, not just on training days. Lever two is progression: the same exercises, made slightly harder over time. One more rep, a slower tempo, a harder variation. Muscle only grows when the signal grows; repeat the exact same signal for ninety days and you have bought maintenance, not growth. Notice what is not a lever: meal timing tricks, fat burners, and suffering. Keep the two real levers moving and the method is almost boring. Boring is good. Boring is what ninety days of compounding looks like from the inside.

beats.text: EVERY DAY, NOT JUST GYM DAYS

beats.title: THE TWO LEVERS
lines: Signal growing. Nothing else matters much.

scenes.narration: Here is the weekly template the method runs on. Three full-body sessions a week: push, pull, squat or hinge, and a carry or core finisher, the same movements every week so progression is measurable. On the days between, walk: a daily step habit is the quiet fat-loss partner that never touches your recovery or your muscle. Once a week, same morning conditions, measure the waist and write it down. Once a month, retake the photos. That is the whole operating system. No six-day splits, no two-hour sessions, no cardio marathons eating the muscle you are trying to build. The template looks almost too simple, and that is precisely why it survives ninety days in a real life with a job, a family and bad weeks. Survival is a feature. The best plan is the one still running on day ninety.

Understand why this road, and not the two famous ones. A bulk on a skinny fat body adds muscle slowly and belly fat quickly, because partitioning is not yet in your favour; most guys end the bulk fatter and start a miserable cut. A cut on a skinny fat body removes fat and the little muscle beneath it at the same time, ending smaller but the same shape. Recomposition is the only road that changes the shape itself: waist down, shoulders up, same scale weight, different person. And your body is uniquely licensed for it. Untrained muscle plus stored energy is the exact combination this method runs on. The guys who bulk and cut are driving around your destination. You are already parked on it. Ninety days of steering, and the shape changes for good.

Now send the signal the method runs on. Push-ups with me, three rounds. Forty seconds on, twenty off, every rep chest to fist height. This front view does not lie about your form. Make each rep one the camera would approve. Go.

The ninety-day rules, all of them. Eat at maintenance or a small deficit, never a crash cut. Hit your protein number daily. Train the same lifts three days a week and progress them in writing. Walk daily. Measure the waist weekly, photos monthly, and judge only by those, never by daily scale noise. Sleep like it is part of the program, because for growth it is. Now the three ways guys wreck this method. They bulk by accident, adding a huge surplus because an app told them to eat big, and the waist grows faster than the shoulders. They cut by panic in week three when the scale has not moved, starving the build they just started. Or they hop programs every fortnight, so no signal ever repeats long enough to compound. Hold the rules, dodge those three, and ninety days is enough to change your shape in photos you can prove.

So, your three numbers, read like a coach. If your push-up max is under fifteen, your first ninety days are mostly about building the signal: strength will climb fast, and the waist will follow. If you are between fifteen and thirty with a waist above half your height, you are the textbook recomp candidate, and both numbers should move every month. If your push-ups are already strong but the waist will not move, your steering is the problem, not your training: audit the surplus you did not know you were eating. Whatever your line says, it says something fixable. Put your waist and your push-up max in the comments. Just the numbers. On day ninety we take the same photos and read them again.

Stop bulking, stop cutting, start steering. Ninety days of signals, protein and patience, and the shape in the photo is a different shape. Your baseline is taken, so the clock is already running. If this way of training makes sense to you, subscribe. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
